                               Steiner-Centroid Pedal Area Ratios
                                       in Elliptic Billiards
                                                     Alper Ferudun∗

                                                     1 October 2026



                                                        Abstract
              For an odd-periodic billiard family between ﬁxed confocal ellipses, we prove that the signed area
          of the original orbit divided by the signed area of its pedal polygon at its own Steiner curvature
          centroid is constant. Both the centroid and this ratio are deﬁned at every real phase. Coprime star
          trajectories and odd repeated traversals are included. Reﬂection identities express the pedal area
          as an isotropic quadratic in the pedal point. Complementary complex pole sets and an odd-degree
          quotient of the Jacobi parameter identify the moving centroid ellipse and reduce the ratio to a
          constant coeﬃcient. A strict theta-function grid inequality proves the necessary nonvanishing in
          the positive-quadratic regime. This establishes invariant k501 of Reznik, Garcia and Koiller. The
          circular case has the elementary value sec2 (πτ /n). No absolute priority claim is made.


1        The original-side Steiner pedal
Fix a > b > 0 and 0 < λ < b2 , and consider the confocal pair

                                      x2 y 2                       x2     y2
                                E:       + 2 = 1,         Eλ :         +       = 1.
                                      a2  b                      a2 − λ b2 − λ
Let P = (Pi )i∈Z/N Z be a billiard polygon on E whose sides are tangent to Eλ . For a cyclic vector
                                ∑
sequence V , write A(V ) = 12 i det(Vi , Vi+1 ). These are signed shoelace areas, including for self-
intersecting stars, not sums of absolute face areas.
    Orient the orbit with its caustic to the left of each edge. Its local turn δi belongs to (0, π); the
internal ray angle is θi = π − δi . Deﬁne the Steiner curvature centroid by
                                      ∑
                                          w i Pi
                                   C = ∑i        ,      wi = sin(2θi ) = − sin(2δi ).                             (1)
                                            i wi

This speciﬁes the angle convention at crossed stars explicitly. Let Qi (M ) be the perpendicular foot of
M on the original supporting sideline Pi Pi+1 , and put

                              A = A(P ),           B(M ) = A(Q(M )),        BC = B(C).

The sidelines here are the original billiard chords, not boundary tangents or the sides of a caustic-
contact polygon.
Theorem 1. For every odd N ≥ 3, the denominator in (1) is nonzero, BC > 0 in the chosen
orientation, and A/BC is independent of the initial vertex in the ﬁxed-caustic billiard family. All
admitted star windings and repeated odd traversals are included.
    ∗
        Mercury Software GmbH. Email: alper@mercurycodelab.com. GitHub: AlperTheKing.


                                                           1
    This is the invariant k501 in Table 6 of Reznik, Garcia and Koiller [1, 2]. Their signed-area and
Steiner-centroid deﬁnitions are retained. Their table says odd N without explicitly requiring least
period; Section 6 explains why repetitions do not require that extra restriction here. Hyperbolic and
degenerate caustics are excluded. Reversing the orbit leaves C unchanged and reverses both areas, so
the ratio is unaﬀected.
    The ﬁxed-polygon Steiner theorem gives circular level sets for pedal area as the pedal point moves;
see [3, §2]. It does not directly give the present ratio: both the original polygon and its own centroid
vary with the billiard phase. The source also observes that the odd-period centroid loci are ellipses.
We prove the precise parametrization of that locus needed here. The Jacobi billiard parametrization is
due to the established theory; we use Stachel’s explicit form [4]. Complex pole cancellation in Poncelet
area problems is also prior methodology [5]. Our argument supplies the original-side pedal trace, the
quotient-torus axis relation, and the strict inequality required to invert the area ratio.

   Finally, (3) shows that q = 0 is equivalent to dn2 ∆ = k 0 . Since dn is strictly decreasing on (0, K)
and dn2 (K/2) = k 0 , this is equivalent to ∆ = K/2, or 4τ = n, impossible for odd n. The same
comparison gives q > 0 precisely when ∆ < K/2.

3    The complementary pole identity
Lemma 3. For odd least period, A(u)S(u) = Λ is a positive constant. The zeros of S are precisely
simple zeros at the shifted Jacobi vertex poles; its poles at the shifted zeros of W are simple.
Proof. The common Jacobi pole positions are zp = 2mK + (2j + 1)iK 0 . The standard shift formulas
[6] give, near iK 0 ,
                                  1                                 i dn w                          i cn w
              sn(iK 0 + w) =          ,    cn(iK 0 + w) = −                ,   dn(iK 0 + w) = −            .
                               k sn w                               k sn w                           sn w
Thus f = dn /W is holomorphic, odd, and zero at each zp . Put Z = zp + K. The point function
satisﬁes P (Z + w) = P (Z − w); at Z = K + iK 0 this follows from
                                              dn w                                  ik 0
                              sn(Z + w) =           ,             cn(Z + w) = −          .
                                             k cn w                               k cn w
The zeros of W are exactly Z ± ∆ modulo 2KZ + 2iK 0 Z. They exhaust its order-two divisor and are
simple: at them
                     sn2 u = α/d,   cn2 u = −β/d,      dn2 u = −λ/(α − λ),                   (12)
so W 0 = −2d sn u cn u dn u 6= 0.
    A shifted W zero can coincide with a shifted vertex pole only if jh = K ± ∆ (mod 2K), or
2τ (2j ± 1) = n(2l + 1). Parity excludes this for odd n. Two diﬀerent indexed vertex poles do not
coincide either, because gcd(2τ, n) = 1. Therefore A has at most simple vertex poles. At each of them
S is analytic and vanishes by pairing its terms under i 7→ n − i, using oddness of f and nh = 4τ K.
The product AS has no pole there.
    At u0 = Z − ∆, the vertices are ﬁnite and Pi (u0 ) = P1−i (u0 ). Reversing the ordered edges thus
gives A(u0 ) = 0. Since S has at most a simple pole there, AS is regular. The other branch is an h
shift; lattice translates preserve the cancellations. These exhaust the possible poles. The entire elliptic
product is constant. On the real locus, each edge has the origin strictly on its left, so det(Pi , Pi+1 ) > 0;
hence A > 0 and Λ = AS > 0.
    At u0 exactly two summands have W poles, at Z − ∆ and Z + ∆. Their residues are equal and
nonzero because f is odd about Z. Thus the pole of S is nonremovable and simple. At every vertex
pole, the zero of S, the at-most-simple pole of A, and AS = Λ 6= 0 force both orders to be exactly one.
The same identity excludes any further zeros of S.


4    The odd quotient torus
Let Q = exp(−πK 0 /K). Choose the unique modulus ℓ ∈ (0, 1) whose nome is Qn , and put

Lemma 4. There are constants A0 , σ > 0 and nonzero real cx , cy such that
                                                σ
                 A = A0 dn(v, ℓ),     S=              ,       Cx = cx sn(v, ℓ),        Cy = cy cn(v, ℓ),       (13)
                                             dn(v, ℓ)
with A0 σ = Λ. Moreover,
                                                q(c2x − c2y )
                                  c − qc2y =                  ,                                                (14)

                                                              4
Proof. Equation (11) and the simple, nonzero residues of S show that Cx , Cy are regular at the shifted
W poles. At Jacobi vertex poles, dn sn /W and dn cn /W are individually holomorphic, while S has a
simple zero. Thus Cx , Cy have at most simple poles at the vertex-pole lattice and no others.
    Put T = 2K/n and E = 2iK 0 . The functions are h-periodic. The characters of (A, Cx , Cy ) under
2K are (+, −, −), and under E they are (−, +, −). The latter follow from the Jacobi characters
(sn, cn, dn) 7→ (sn, − cn, − dn). Choose integers r, t with 2τ r + nt = 1. Since n is odd, t is odd, and
T = rh + t(2K) also has characters (+, −, −).
    All possible vertex poles form the one class iK 0 modulo T Z + EZ. Under u 7→ v, T maps to
2L and iK 0 to iL0 . The functions dn(v, ℓ), sn(v, ℓ), cn(v, ℓ) have respectively the same characters and
simple-pole class. Subtract from each of A, Cx , Cy a multiple of the appropriate function to cancel the
residue at iK 0 . The characters cancel every translated residue. The diﬀerence is entire with periods
2T, 2E, hence constant, and a negative character forces that constant to vanish. This proves the
asserted representations, initially allowing a zero axis scale. Evaluation at zero gives A0 = A(0) > 0,
and Lemma 3 gives σ = S(0) > 0. Evaluation at real phases where the Jacobi functions are nonzero
shows cx , cy are real.
    At u0 = K + iK 0 − ∆, the two branch values of sn and cn are equal, by evenness about K + iK 0 .
Taking the ratios of residues in (11) and (6) gives
                                        a(β − λ) sn u0                        b(α − λ) cn u0
                         Cx (u0 ) = −                  ,       Cy (u0 ) =                    .                (16)
                                             2βq                                   2αq
Both coordinates are nonzero. Equation (12) and the factorization

    α4 (β − λ)2 − β 4 (α − λ)2
                                                                                                 [                ]
                                                                                  = d(D − λs) sD − λ(α2 + β 2 )

show C(u0 ) · C(u0 ) = c/q. Now v(u0 ) = (n − 2τ )L + iL0 , with n − 2τ odd. Its squared Jacobi values
are sn2 (v, ℓ) = 1/ℓ2 and cn2 (v, ℓ) = −ℓ02 /ℓ2 . Substitution proves (14). Taking the ratio of squared
coordinates in (16) proves (15), using k 02 = (β − λ)/(α − λ) and (3). It also proves both axis scales
nonzero.

     From (13), (14), and sn2 v + cn2 v = 1 we obtain
                                     q(c2x − c2y ) 2                     BC   Hσ 2 q(c2x − c2y )
                      c − q(C · C) =              dn (v, ℓ),                =                    .            (17)
                                          ℓ2                             A          ℓ2 Λ
This already proves constancy of the reciprocal ratio. Nonvanishing is a separate obligation: it is not
legitimate to invert a constant that might be zero.


5      A strict odd-grid inequality and nonvanishing
                                                                                     0
Lemma 5. Let 0 < k < 1, and let ℓ have nome Qn , where Q = e−πK /K and n ≥ 5 is odd. If τ is a
positive integer with ∆ = 2τ K/n < K/2, then
                                                                k 02
                                                 dn4 (∆, k) >        .                                        (18)
                                                                 ℓ0
Proof. Deﬁne F (x) = log dn(Kx/π, k) − 21 log k 0 . The half-period identity dn(u + K) = k 0 / dn u gives
F (x + π) = −F (x), and F is even. On [0, π/2] it is decreasing, positive before the right endpoint, and
F (π/2) = 0. It is strictly concave in the interior: with z = sn2 u,

                          (log dn u)00 = −                           <0     (0 < u < K/2).

Indeed dn u = k 0 θ3 (πu/(2K), Q)/θ4 (πu/(2K), Q), and expanding log((1 + z)/(1 − z)) in the paired
products gives (19). Summation over the odd n-grid gives

                             ∑

The grid factor n cancels the denominator of the surviving frequency nm.
    Put t = π/n, r = bn/4c, and dj = F ((j − 1)t) − F (jt). Strict concavity implies d2j > d2j−1 for the
indices used below. Folding the grid with evenness and F (π − x) = −F (x) gives

                                                      ∑
                                                      r
                      n = 4r + 1 : G = F (0) − 2               d2j < F (2rt),
                                                      j=1
                                                      ∑r
                      n = 4r + 3 : G = F (0) − 2               d2j − 2F ((2r + 1)t) < F (2rt).
                                                      j=1

In the second line (2r + 1)t < π/2, so the extra term is strictly negative. The assumption implies
τ ≤ r. Thus F (2τ t) ≥ F (2rt) > G > G/2. Equations (20) and the deﬁnition of F now give
4 log dn ∆ − 2 log k 0 > − log ℓ0 , proving (18).

Completion of Theorem 1. The centroid is ﬁnite by Lemma 2. If q < 0, (7) immediately gives BC =
HS(c − q|C|2 ) > 0 at every real phase. If q > 0, then ∆ < K/2; in particular n ≥ 5. Lemma 5 and
(15) give c2x > c2y . Formula (17) is therefore strictly positive in this case too. Its inverse is the desired
constant A/BC .


6    Boundary cases, veriﬁcation and scope
If a listed odd orbit of length N repeats an orbit of least period n, then N = mn forces n, m odd.
Both weight sums in (1) are multiplied by m, so C is unchanged. Both areas are multiplied by m, and
their ratio is unchanged. This proves the repeated-traversal assertion without narrowing the source’s
odd-length condition.
    For a = b, the primitive trajectory is a regular star with chord step 2πτ /n. Its common weight
is − sin(4πτ /n), nonzero for odd n, and C = O. The feet form a rotated similar star scaled by
cos(πτ /n) > 0, giving A/BC = sec2 (πτ /n). For n = 3 on a general ellipse, the Steiner centroid is
the triangle circumcenter and its feet are the three side midpoints, yielding the familiar ratio 4. This
classical case is not claimed as new.
    The supporting package retains exact coeﬃcient checks and low-period geometric controls. It also
retains numerical tests with their arithmetic precision, geometry residuals, and rejected integrations.
These support regression testing, not the all-period theorem, whose proof is analytic above. In par-
ticular, positivity of the stationary pedal area of an arbitrary ellipse-inscribed polygon is false; that
tempting shortcut is not used here.
    Only the original-side own-Steiner ratio k501 is claimed. The neighboring outer and inner invariants
k502 , k503 and hyperbolic or degenerate caustics are not addressed. A bounded primary-literature

search did not identify an earlier proof of the same all-odd statement; this does not establish exhaustive
novelty or absolute priority. This unrefereed manuscript was developed with AI assistance in the

is responsible for its claims. No independent human review or formal proof-assistant veriﬁcation is
asserted.
